A little reverberation may help us follow speech. Hearing researchers at Macquarie University in Sydney have shown how the brain learns to “listen to the room.” In the study, funded by the Australian Research Council and published in eLife, normal-hearing volunteers in the university’s anechoic chamber heard recordings simulating spaces such as an underground car park, a lecture hall and an open-plan office, with varying reverberation. They reported short spoken commands heard against background noise. Animal brains were known to adapt quickly to changes in sound level; this is the first study to show humans adapting to reverberant spaces to understand speech.

Participants improved over time even in difficult rooms, said senior author Distinguished Professor David McAlpine, but learned best in a “Goldilocks zone” of about 400 ms of reverberation, typical of modern lecture halls. Very echoey spaces hindered learning, and so, unexpectedly, did rooms with no echo at all. The sweet spot matches the average reverberation of the spaces we spend most time in: either we build for our brains, or our brains have adapted to our buildings.

First author Dr. Heivet Hernández-Pérez said the brain learns the structure of an environment without our noticing: “our ears hear, but our brains listen.” Briefly disrupting a learning-related brain region with magnetic stimulation sharply reduced adaptation, pointing to dedicated circuits. Hearing aids and headphones that strip out all reverberation, McAlpine warns, may discard something the brain finds useful. Next come studies of neurodivergent listeners and people with hearing loss.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from an article in The Lighthouse, Macquarie University’s news site (August 2025). Read the original.
